payload.text: Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo , which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital , Isai and Ternel . The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments. Exits Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities. Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets , a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February. On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November. Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing. payload.text: More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots. Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1 , the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low. Smaller Series B rounds grow scarcer One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds. So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data. The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set. Big rounds still a big thing On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular. At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals. Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus , Jeff Bezos ’ physical AI startup that launched last year. Model developer World Labs , led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li , was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor. For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients. Mostly an AI story Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group. So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories. AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies. Bullish climate for Series B Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed. Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies. payload.text: Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning. U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done. Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase . Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020. Size your seed against the Series A Uncork Capital ‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal. A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic , a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed , right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures , then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later. Map your Series A leads now Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything. Sell your way to the bar The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion. At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine. From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside. A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one. As the co-founder and managing partner of MGV , Marc Schröder is committed to establishing MGV as the premier venture firm for world-class tech entrepreneurs to accelerate their visions. Under Schröder’s stewardship, MGV has swiftly ascended to a top-quartile firm, surpassing the performance of 95% of venture funds. Business Insider has recognized him as one of the Top 100 global seed investors , and his perspectives are published regularly in Crunchbase News and other leading publications. payload.text: Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels. Rebekah Johnson, founder and CEO of Numericle. (Courtesy photo) The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation. The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected. Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents. Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers. For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning. Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone. From a regulatory warning to a company Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West , said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission ’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016. She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling. About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen. “Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking. Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle. She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes. “When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said. That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A. Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare. The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers. Verifying increasingly convincing fakes Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls. Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers. A business call from Numeracle, delivered with name, logo, and reason for calling. (Photo courtesy of Numeracle) Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam. AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles. “The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.” She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail. Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort. The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call. Investor POV: ‘Doing more with less’ For Lenard Marcus , a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers. He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.” Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales. Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said. “She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added. Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent. “This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said. payload.text: I got off the phone with a potential client whose company is doing great. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph. payload.text: Editor’s note: The following is the latest profile in a series of articles about startup founders from non-technical backgrounds who have launched successful venture-backed companies. Read the previous interviews in the series including with MagicSchool AI founder Adeel Khan here , Trunk Tools founder Sarah Buchner here , Tabs founder Ali Hussain here , Craft founder Ilya Levtov here , GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti here , Incredible Health co-founder Iman Abuzeid here , and Hilt founder William “Will” Cielen here . Lilly Chen was 16 and had been repeatedly hospitalized for Graves’ disease when her mother suggested they move to China and become monks. Frustrated with the care her daughter was receiving through Medicaid, she wanted to try something different. Lilly Chen, co-founder and CEO of FSH Technologies. (Courtesy photo) Chen left high school and spent about two years as a monk, ordained in the United States before spending several months at a monastery in China. She meditated, reread the same books, and gradually felt well enough to consider returning to school. She went on to enter Colorado College without a high school diploma, briefly play video games professionally, and become an engineer at Facebook . When she quit that job, she didn’t have a startup idea. She just wanted to find work she believed in. That mission eventually led her to FSH (pronounced “fish) Technologies ,” a Philadelphia-based company that’s building software for some of the government’s least glamorous tasks, including administering school food services and managing public records. After her brief stint at a large tech company, Chen realized she wanted to tackle the everyday problems that make people’s lives harder, even if solving them wouldn’t generate much excitement in Silicon Valley. “What does it actually take to solve the really unsexy, boring stuff?” she remembers asking herself. A different route to college Before Chen was thinking about government software, she was trying to get well enough to return to school. At the monastery in China, she meditated, ate food grown on-site or brought by nearby villagers, and lived without internet access. She continued taking thyroid medication and said her health became more manageable during that period. She also read. A lot. With no nearby place to buy books, she reread the ones she had brought, finding different places around the monastery to sit with them. Her attachment to those books prompted a conversation with a fellow monk who asked what she enjoyed about reading and where she might find more books. The discussion eventually turned to colleges, and why she wasn’t attending one. Chen explained her health problems. He observed that she seemed well. She realized she was. So Chen returned to the U.S., homeschooled herself and enrolled at Colorado College without having earned a high school diploma. She turned 20 during her freshman year and graduated in 2019 with a double major in mathematics and economics. While she was in college, Chen briefly played Dota 2 professionally. She also played against OpenAI ’s game-playing bots, an early encounter with AI technology she would later help support as an engineer. After an initial job in Boston, she joined Facebook, where she built infrastructure used to train AI models. Leaving without a startup idea Then on Jan. 6, 2021, Chen was attending a remote company all-hands meeting while watching coverage of the attack on the U.S. Capitol on another screen. Her concerns about Facebook’s role in enabling the organization of violence made her question whether she could continue working there. “I realized that I couldn’t work for Big Tech anymore,” she recalls. She quit shortly afterward. To figure out her next move, she returned to the sort of questions she had encountered as a monk. What made her happy? What mattered to her? What was she good at? Programming remained her most concrete skill. She just needed to figure out where to apply it. An introduction through Envision , a student-run accelerator focused on nontraditional founders, connected her with Contrary , a venture firm that has backed the likes of Ramp and Anduril Industries . The firm wrote Chen her first check in 2021, before she had even settled on the business that would become FSH. Although she didn’t have a developed company pitch, Chen’s earnest explanation of what motivated her and her passion for solving a meaningful problem won investors over. That investment gave her room to experiment, she said. FSH took shape into what it is today in 2024. The Contrary investor who first backed her, Jason Chen , has since joined the company as its chief operating officer. The company has raised $25 million in total funding, including a recent $20 million Series A that Chen said came together in about a week. Participants in that raise included Lachy Groom , General Catalyst , Ramp, Scribble Ventures , Operator Partners , Basis Set Ventures . Contrary also led its seed financing. Finding the problem beneath the paperwork Ultimately, Chen landed on government software because in her view, it had the potential to solve many consequential problems that attracted relatively little excitement. For example, permits, licenses, grant applications and other administrative processes can be slow for reasons that extend beyond an outdated interface, Chen noted. Information may exist in separate departments. Updating a website may require approvals from multiple stakeholders including policymakers, communications staff and an IT team. Putting a chatbot on top of that system, Chen argues, leaves much of the underlying problem unresolved. Her approach to solving some of the problems that exist within governments draws on an exchange she had years earlier at the monastery, where one of her chores was feeding koi. The head monk would periodically ask her if she thought she was the fish or the pond? Initially, Chen didn’t understand what he was asking. But he kept returning to the question, and she began thinking about it. Eventually, she picked a fish she thought resembled her: one that stayed out of fights, swam with the group and occasionally ventured off on its own. The head monk’s response was, “You’re the pond, not the fish.” Chen viewed the exchange as a lesson in looking beyond individual pieces to understand how a whole system works. Looking at government software, she believed that it meant examining why information is scattered or processes are slow before deciding what technology to build. One early area for FSH has been K-12 food services, where administrators must perform tasks such as coordinating meal planning, nutritional information and reimbursement requirements. Another is records and archive management, including the paper documents that can still require residents to visit a government office to retrieve them. FSH does use AI for tasks such as optical character recognition, translation and natural-language search. But, Chen said, the company treats it as a tool within its software, rather than relying on a chatbot or an AI agent to handle an entire process. Government sales have required patience. The company generated less than $100,000 in revenue in its first year, Chen said, reflecting the time it takes to win contracts. At the time of this interview, FSH had roughly eight or nine employees, with additional offers outstanding. Thinking slowly, moving quickly Chen’s time as a monk has also influenced how she runs the company. She admits she is skeptical of startup culture that treats sleeping in the office or working extremely long hours as evidence of commitment or a badge of pride. Rather, Chen views some of that behavior as performative, especially when it comes at the expense of the rest that she believes people need to work effectively. Her preferred motto to the team is, “Slow is smooth and smooth is fast.” “We think slowly about a lot of things, and then we do things quickly,” she said. Chen believes it’s crucial to first understand the people, departments and procedures behind a government service before trying to improve it. Looking back, Chen also credits her success to finding people willing to back someone whose experience didn’t resemble the usual résumé. That includes the college that admitted her without a high school diploma and an investor who wrote a check before she had settled on a company idea. “You definitely end up finding your own way if you just stick to being weird,” she said. payload.text: Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three  years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. title: Cdn
summary:
前几天，我在一个平台发了条动态，预告自己在做的一个写作发布工具。底下有人说没啥用，不如做个抢优惠券的；也有人说别自嗨。

我没有生气，也没往心里去，但它让我想了很久。平台上的读者来自四面八方，关心的东西差别很大，同一件事在不同的人眼里，价值完全不同，这很正常。我真正在意的是另一件事：我想写的东西，是不是只能放进推荐流里，等一个不确定的结果？

这让我重新审视了一个老问题：在 AI 时代，个人博客还有什么位置，能起什么作用。

先说难听的：我知道现在开独立博客很傻。

平台有推荐，AI 有摘要，人连搜索结果都懒得点。新域名没有权重，没有外链，没有推荐位，写一篇长文发出去，阅读量个位数是常态。这不是“内容不够好”的问题，是分发结构就这样。所以问题不是“博客还有没有价值”，而是：**在一个人人都不直接访问网站的时代，我为什么还要建一个自己的站？**

![site-home-light]( https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/kingshuaishuai/ys-imgs@main/quirepub/4dfc71519187e9dc8176a7145ec7e6a4.png)
*yishuai.wang 的首页。*

这看起来确实像 49 年入国军。

## 这个比喻，成立一半

成立的一半是：**如果把独立站当流量生意做，那它就是逆风局。** 靠 SEO 等自然流量、靠广告联盟变现、靠批量更新维持权重——这套玩法在 AI 把内容供给打到无限之后，基本没有胜算。AI 一秒能生成的通稿，你写十篇也没人看，搜索引擎也未必收录。这个意义上，49 年入国军不是玩笑。

不成立的一半是：**49 年入国军是押注一个正在崩塌的旧秩序；我不是押注“独立博客会重新成为流量中心”。** 我不认为独立站会回到 2010 年那种“写博客—被搜索引擎收录—拿流量—接广告”的黄金年代。那个年代确实结束了。

我押的是另一件事：**AI 内容越泛滥，一手经历、真实项目、可验证署名，可能越稀缺。**

现在下结论还太早。AI 可以帮我查资料、改代码、润色句子，但它没有做过我做的项目，没有踩过我踩的坑，没有在四个月里对着分页排版一个像素一个像素地改。它写不出“我当时为什么决定不用现成方案”这种判断，因为它没有“当时”。但这套东西到底有没有人认，我不知道，只能先做再看。

## 不是没人读，可能是阅读结构变了

“AI 时代少有人类阅读”这句话对一半。更准确地说：**人直接访问一个陌生独立站的概率变低了，但人通过 AI 搜索、AI 摘要、GitHub 、开发者社区、RSS 找到你的路径，可能变多了。**

读者未必消失，入口可能在变。以前入口是搜索引擎结果页，现在入口可能是：

- 有人问 AI“中文分页编辑器怎么做”，AI 引用了你的文章；
- 有人在 GitHub 看到 QuireKit ，顺藤摸瓜找到你的站；
- 有人从 V2EX 、即刻、X 、掘金看到一段踩坑记录，点进来看完整版；
- 有人用 RSS 订阅了你的站，每篇都读，但从不留言。

这些都不体现在“首页访问量”里。但这也只是我的观察，不一定对。还有一个坑必须说清楚：**被 AI 读到 ≠ 被 AI 引用 ≠ 被 AI 导流。** 放一个 `llms.txt` 就以为 AI 会替你传播，是自我安慰。llms.txt 不是标准，很多 AI 不读，读了也不一定引用；被训练进模型更不等于有人会来你的站。所以我没把 llms.txt 当战略，只当导览。我试图做的是：**让站更像一个可被引用的一手源，并且尽量确保引用里有我的名字、链接和工具。** 做不做得成，另说。

## 还有一些很个人的原因

yishuai.wang 就是我的名字。我很喜欢这个域名，只是一直没好好用起来。

这几年在各个平台发文，我也有个感受：有些平台越来越平台化，推荐、热榜、流量规则排在前面，技术本身反而退到了后面。V2EX 是我觉得一直保持初心的地方，也是给我帮助最多的社区。如果有一天有机会，我也想在国内做一个像它这样的社区。现在还很远，先从把自己的站写好开始。

所以我重新把站点搭了起来，也终于把这个域名用上了。给自己留一块净土：不用围着推荐规则写，想写什么就写什么。

## 我正在尝试的事

都是很具体、也还没验证的事。

**第一，写我想写的，但让站里有一部分内容有“为什么是我”。** 我会写工程记录，也会写随笔、观点、工具分享。这些内容别人也能写，我不装作每篇都有独家价值。但站里得有一部分是别人替代不了的：QuireKit 的工程记录、分页排版的踩坑、为什么不用现成方案、四个月做到 Word 常用功能 85% 兼容是什么过程。这些不是每篇都有，但它们决定了这个站“为什么是我”。其余内容自由写，写得开心就写，只是我不拿它们当护城河。

![site-article]( https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/kingshuaishuai/ys-imgs@main/quirepub/1d5b58c6e0b6451f96b8cc13fc5c3aee.png)
*文章页：开头是智能总结，右侧是目录，每篇都能直接拿到 Markdown 原文。*

**第四，保留 RSS 。** 独立站没有平台推荐，RSS 是我能想到的少数真正属于我的连接：不经过算法，更新了就能收到。中文、英文和全部内容各有一个订阅源。有没有人用，还要再看。

## 这个站，是用我自己做的工具搭的

我清楚 QuireKit 是什么、能做什么，所以愿意自己先吃这份 dogfood：这个站就是用它搭的。

QuireKit 是我在做的开源文档编辑器生态。主打的是 Classic 分页文档编辑器：在浏览器里真正分页，断行、分页、光标、选区都自己算，像 Word 、WPS 一样一页一页地编辑；另一条线是 MSFE ，专为 Markdown 定制的编辑器框架，Markdown 原文就是文档。

yishuai.wang 从页面到写作，用的都是它：

- 页面用 QuireKit 的组件库和 InkWash 水墨主题；
- 写文章的后台和评论框都是 MD Editor （基于 MSFE ），文档、实时预览、源码三种视图随时切换；
- 每篇文章在地址后面加 `.md` 就能拿到原文，配上中英文 RSS 、canonical 、`llms.txt`，就是上面说的“可引用的结构”；
- 文章开头的智能总结在发布后生成一次，读者阅读时不会调用模型；
- 站点也支持 Micropub ，以后可以从别的写作工具直接发文到站上。

![site-comment]( https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/kingshuaishuai/ys-imgs@main/quirepub/522d5267e115070825c6835a4603e7b5.png)
*评论框就是 MD Editor ，页脚是 RSS 和 llms.txt 。*

站点源码也开源了（ MIT ）：[https://github.com/kingshuaishuai/yishuai.wang](<https://github.com/kingshuaishuai/yishuai.wang>) 。自己的东西先自己用，哪里不顺手，最先知道的是我。

## 所以，是 49 年入国军吗

**我认为不是。但这只是我的个人观点，不构成对任何人的建议。**

国军押的是一套正在崩塌的秩序；我押的是另一件事：**当 AI 把内容供给打到无限，人的经历、判断、署名和可验证的一手记录，可能会变贵。** 独立站可能没人看，但它至少是我留给自己的一个源头。域名、文章和版本记录归我，不被平台算法拿捏，也不被 AI 摘要一笔带过。

还有一层原因。好的中文技术博客本来就不多，而大模型能答成什么样，很大程度上取决于它能读到什么。如果资料大多是搬运和水文，模型再强，也会被这样的资料生态限制住。一个人的站很渺小，像一颗星；但好的内容生态，本来就是很多颗星组成的。我想做其中一颗。

没人看是常态，不是判决。我先写一批只有我能写的东西，再写更多我想写的东西，然后看它值不值得活下去。

AI 可以读它、引用它、忽略它。但源头在这里。

至于这是不是 49 年入国军——我现在不知道。我只是觉得，与其等一个确定的答案，不如先把自己的那一份留下来。

---

现在下结论还太早。AI 可以帮我查资料、改代码、润色句子，但它没有做过我做的项目，没有踩过我踩的坑，没有在四个月里对着分页排版一个像素一个像素地改。它写不出“我当时为什么决定不用现成方案”这种判断，因为它没有“当时”。但这套东西到底有没有人认，我不知道，只能先做再看。

不是没人读，可能是阅读结构变了

“AI 时代少有人类阅读”这句话对一半。更准确地说：人直接访问一个陌生独立站的概率变低了，但人通过 AI 搜索、AI 摘要、GitHub 、开发者社区、RSS 找到你的路径，可能变多了。

读者未必消失，入口可能在变。以前入口是搜索引擎结果页，现在入口可能是：

  • 有人问 AI“中文分页编辑器怎么做”，AI 引用了你的文章；
  • 有人在 GitHub 看到 QuireKit ，顺藤摸瓜找到你的站；
  • 有人从 V2EX 、即刻、X 、掘金看到一段踩坑记录，点进来看完整版；
  • 有人用 RSS 订阅了你的站，每篇都读，但从不留言。

这些都不体现在“首页访问量”里。但这也只是我的观察，不一定对。还有一个坑必须说清楚：被 AI 读到 ≠ 被 AI 引用 ≠ 被 AI 导流。 放一个 llms.txt 就以为 AI 会替你传播，是自我安慰。llms.txt 不是标准，很多 AI 不读，读了也不一定引用；被训练进模型更不等于有人会来你的站。所以我没把 llms.txt 当战略，只当导览。我试图做的是：让站更像一个可被引用的一手源，并且尽量确保引用里有我的名字、链接和工具。 做不做得成，另说。

还有一些很个人的原因

yishuai.wang 就是我的名字。我很喜欢这个域名，只是一直没好好用起来。

这几年在各个平台发文，我也有个感受：有些平台越来越平台化，推荐、热榜、流量规则排在前面，技术本身反而退到了后面。V2EX 是我觉得一直保持初心的地方，也是给我帮助最多的社区。如果有一天有机会，我也想在国内做一个像它这样的社区。现在还很远，先从把自己的站写好开始。

所以我重新把站点搭了起来，也终于把这个域名用上了。给自己留一块净土：不用围着推荐规则写，想写什么就写什么。

我正在尝试的事

都是很具体、也还没验证的事。

第一，写我想写的，但让站里有一部分内容有“为什么是我”。 我会写工程记录，也会写随笔、观点、工具分享。这些内容别人也能写，我不装作每篇都有独家价值。但站里得有一部分是别人替代不了的：QuireKit 的工程记录、分页排版的踩坑、为什么不用现成方案、四个月做到 Word 常用功能 85% 兼容是什么过程。这些不是每篇都有，但它们决定了这个站“为什么是我”。其余内容自由写，写得开心就写，只是我不拿它们当护城河。

第二，让独立站做首发站。 以后文章先发在 yishuai.wang ，再同步到各个平台，平台上也是完整内容，不做删减。之后有修改和补充，先更新站内版本。能设 canonical 的平台就指向站内原文，不能设的就在文末写一句“本文首发并持续更新于 yishuai.wang”。

第三，给 AI 和人准备可引用的结构。 长文里补结论卡、事实表、FAQ 、版本记录；给 QuireKit 单独做工具页，写清楚一句话定义、功能、边界、许可证、对比、路线图。AI 最爱抽取的通常不是长叙事，是结论、事实、版本、对比、代码和边界。工具页可能比博客文章更容易被 AI 推荐。这只是假设，我按这个假设在做。

文章页：开头是智能总结，右侧是目录，每篇都能直接拿到 Markdown 原文。

第四，保留 RSS 。 独立站没有平台推荐，RSS 是我能想到的少数真正属于我的连接：不经过算法，更新了就能收到。中文、英文和全部内容各有一个订阅源。有没有人用，还要再看。

第五，不和 AI 对抗，把 AI 当一层分发。 我不指望拦着 AI 读我的站，也拦不住。我能做的是让 AI 读到的内容是可验证的、有署名的、有链接的。AI 的输出有人看，那我希望那个输出里，有我的名字和我的工具。

这个站，是用我自己做的工具搭的

我清楚 QuireKit 是什么、能做什么，所以愿意自己先吃这份 dogfood：这个站就是用它搭的。

QuireKit 是我在做的开源文档编辑器生态。主打的是 Classic 分页文档编辑器：在浏览器里真正分页，断行、分页、光标、选区都自己算，像 Word 、WPS 一样一页一页地编辑；另一条线是 MSFE ，专为 Markdown 定制的编辑器框架，Markdown 原文就是文档。

yishuai.wang 从页面到写作，用的都是它：

  • 页面用 QuireKit 的组件库和 InkWash 水墨主题；
  • 写文章的后台和评论框都是 MD Editor （基于 MSFE ），文档、实时预览、源码三种视图随时切换；
  • 每篇文章在地址后面加 .md 就能拿到原文，配上中英文 RSS 、canonical 、llms.txt，就是上面说的“可引用的结构”；
  • 文章开头的智能总结在发布后生成一次，读者阅读时不会调用模型；
  • 站点也支持 Micropub ，以后可以从别的写作工具直接发文到站上。

评论框就是 MD Editor ，页脚是 RSS 和 llms.txt 。

站点源码也开源了（ MIT ）：https://github.com/kingshuaishuai/yishuai.wang 。自己的东西先自己用，哪里不顺手，最先知道的是我。

所以，是 49 年入国军吗

我认为不是。但这只是我的个人观点，不构成对任何人的建议。

国军押的是一套正在崩塌的秩序；我押的是另一件事：当 AI 把内容供给打到无限，人的经历、判断、署名和可验证的一手记录，可能会变贵。 独立站可能没人看，但它至少是我留给自己的一个源头。域名、文章和版本记录归我，不被平台算法拿捏，也不被 AI 摘要一笔带过。

还有一层原因。好的中文技术博客本来就不多，而大模型能答成什么样，很大程度上取决于它能读到什么。如果资料大多是搬运和水文，模型再强，也会被这样的资料生态限制住。一个人的站很渺小，像一颗星；但好的内容生态，本来就是很多颗星组成的。我想做其中一颗。

没人看是常态，不是判决。我先写一批只有我能写的东西，再写更多我想写的东西，然后看它值不值得活下去。

AI 可以读它、引用它、忽略它。但源头在这里。

至于这是不是 49 年入国军——我现在不知道。我只是觉得，与其等一个确定的答案，不如先把自己的那一份留下来。

本文首发并持续更新于 yishuai.wang。

title: Terryhu
summary:
## 个人网站即我的世界

过去我是个喜欢折腾网站的人，但模板换了又换，总感觉被什么东西困住了。

受我的世界、黑客帝国和元宇宙的启发，借助 AI ，我把个人网站从二维网页建成了三维世界。

这个世界包罗万象，可以自由移动，里面建了篮球场，健身房，工作台，甚至还有昼夜交替和天气系统。

对于二维网页也完全可以内嵌进来，例如按 F 查看。而且得益于方块风的性能开销小，手机也能轻松访问。

逛上一圈，像是去朋友家做客了一趟。比起传统的网站，这样的相识或许更让人印象深刻。

一旦接受了这个设定，就再也回不去传统个人网站了…

title: Marketplace
summary:
大家好，最近做了一个 VS Code 插件 **SeekDock**，想在这里分享一下。

项目的初衷是希望把 DeepSeek Harness（DSH）的 Agent 能力集成到 VS Code 中，让 AI 不只是回答问题，还能直接参与日常开发工作，比如读写代码、执行命令、搜索文件、浏览网页等。

项目目前是 0.1.0 版本，MIT 开源，属于社区非官方扩展。

**项目地址：**

- VS Code Marketplace： https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=JerryHu.seekdock
- GitHub： https://github.com/jerryhu/seekdock

### 一、侧边栏里的 AI Agent

SeekDock 将聊天面板放在 VS Code 右侧辅助侧边栏，不需要切换窗口，可以一边查看代码，一边与 Agent 对话。

支持三种打开方式：

- 编辑器右上角图标
- 快捷键：macOS `Cmd+Alt+L`，Windows/Linux `Ctrl+Alt+L`
- 命令面板：`SeekDock: Open SeekDock`

内置 DeepSeek Harness 运行时，不需要额外安装 Python、CLI 或单独启动服务。安装插件后，配置自己的 DeepSeek API Key 即可使用。

### 二、Agent 不只是聊天，还能执行任务

支持多种工具调用：

- 读取、创建、修改文件
- 搜索文件和代码
- 执行终端命令
- 浏览网页、访问 URL
- 使用 Skills 扩展 Agent 能力
- 通过 MCP 接入外部工具和服务

工具调用过程会以卡片形式展示，可以展开查看参数、执行结果和输出内容。

回答支持流式输出，思考过程可以折叠展示，任务执行过程中也可以随时停止。

### 三、四档权限控制，避免 AI 随意修改代码

这是我比较重视的一个功能。

SeekDock 提供四种权限模式：

- **仅可查看**：只允许读取文件，不允许修改。
- **工作区内修改**：允许修改当前工作区文件，超出范围需要审批。
- **完全权限**：减少确认步骤，可以执行敏感操作，启用前需要风险确认。
- **自动审查（实验）**：每次工具调用前由模型进行审查，拒绝的操作再交给用户决定。

需要审批时，会在对应的工具卡片上显示，可以选择「允许一次」或「拒绝」。

默认采用 fail-closed 策略，没有可用的审批响应时不会自动放行。

### 四、代码修改有记录，可以查看 Diff

Agent 完成一轮任务后，会展示文件修改情况：

- 显示修改了多少个文件。
- 显示每个文件增加和删除的代码行数。
- 悬停文件可以预览 Diff。
- 点击文件可以使用 VS Code 原生 Diff 查看修改前后的区别。
- 历史会话重新打开后，也可以查看之前的修改记录。

这样不仅能让 AI 修改代码，也方便开发者检查 AI 到底改了什么。

### 五、Skills、计划模式和 MCP

**Skills**

支持搜索和多选 Skills，通过 `/` 调用，可以管理工作区和用户级技能。

**计划模式**

可以先让 Agent 分析需求、拆解任务并生成实施计划，确认后再执行，适合相对复杂的开发任务。

**MCP**

支持 stdio 和 Streamable HTTP 两种连接方式，可以配置环境变量、请求头和密钥，也支持从 Codex、Claude、Cursor 等工具导入已有 MCP 配置。

### 六、其他功能

- 会话管理：查看、恢复、重命名和删除历史会话。
- 模型切换：支持 Flash / Pro，以及不同推理强度。
- 文件引用：可以在消息中添加工作区文件作为上下文。
- Markdown：支持 Markdown 渲染和代码块一键复制。

payload.title: 做了一个 VS Code 插件：把 DeepSeek Harness Agent 放进侧边栏，支持权限控制和 Diff 追踪
payload.content:
大家好，最近做了一个 VS Code 插件 **SeekDock**，想在这里分享一下。

项目的初衷是希望把 DeepSeek Harness（DSH）的 Agent 能力集成到 VS Code 中，让 AI 不只是回答问题，还能直接参与日常开发工作，比如读写代码、执行命令、搜索文件、浏览网页等。

项目目前是 0.1.0 版本，MIT 开源，属于社区非官方扩展。

**项目地址：**

- VS Code Marketplace： https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=JerryHu.seekdock
- GitHub： https://github.com/jerryhu/seekdock

### 一、侧边栏里的 AI Agent

SeekDock 将聊天面板放在 VS Code 右侧辅助侧边栏，不需要切换窗口，可以一边查看代码，一边与 Agent 对话。

支持三种打开方式：

- 编辑器右上角图标
- 快捷键：macOS `Cmd+Alt+L`，Windows/Linux `Ctrl+Alt+L`
- 命令面板：`SeekDock: Open SeekDock`

内置 DeepSeek Harness 运行时，不需要额外安装 Python、CLI 或单独启动服务。安装插件后，配置自己的 DeepSeek API Key 即可使用。

### 二、Agent 不只是聊天，还能执行任务

支持多种工具调用：

- 读取、创建、修改文件
- 搜索文件和代码
- 执行终端命令
- 浏览网页、访问 URL
- 使用 Skills 扩展 Agent 能力
- 通过 MCP 接入外部工具和服务

工具调用过程会以卡片形式展示，可以展开查看参数、执行结果和输出内容。

回答支持流式输出，思考过程可以折叠展示，任务执行过程中也可以随时停止。

### 三、四档权限控制，避免 AI 随意修改代码

这是我比较重视的一个功能。

SeekDock 提供四种权限模式：

- **仅可查看**：只允许读取文件，不允许修改。
- **工作区内修改**：允许修改当前工作区文件，超出范围需要审批。
- **完全权限**：减少确认步骤，可以执行敏感操作，启用前需要风险确认。
- **自动审查（实验）**：每次工具调用前由模型进行审查，拒绝的操作再交给用户决定。

需要审批时，会在对应的工具卡片上显示，可以选择「允许一次」或「拒绝」。

默认采用 fail-closed 策略，没有可用的审批响应时不会自动放行。

### 四、代码修改有记录，可以查看 Diff

Agent 完成一轮任务后，会展示文件修改情况：

- 显示修改了多少个文件。
- 显示每个文件增加和删除的代码行数。
- 悬停文件可以预览 Diff。
- 点击文件可以使用 VS Code 原生 Diff 查看修改前后的区别。
- 历史会话重新打开后，也可以查看之前的修改记录。

这样不仅能让 AI 修改代码，也方便开发者检查 AI 到底改了什么。

### 五、Skills、计划模式和 MCP

**Skills**

支持搜索和多选 Skills，通过 `/` 调用，可以管理工作区和用户级技能。

**计划模式**

可以先让 Agent 分析需求、拆解任务并生成实施计划，确认后再执行，适合相对复杂的开发任务。

**MCP**

支持 stdio 和 Streamable HTTP 两种连接方式，可以配置环境变量、请求头和密钥，也支持从 Codex、Claude、Cursor 等工具导入已有 MCP 配置。

### 六、其他功能

- 会话管理：查看、恢复、重命名和删除历史会话。
- 模型切换：支持 Flash / Pro，以及不同推理强度。
- 文件引用：可以在消息中添加工作区文件作为上下文。
- Markdown：支持 Markdown 渲染和代码块一键复制。
- 多语言：支持简体中文、繁体中文、英语、日语等 10 种界面语言。
- API Key：使用 VS Code SecretStorage 安全保存，不写入普通配置文件。

### 七、安装和使用

1. 在 VS Code Marketplace 搜索 `SeekDock` 并安装。
2. 使用 `Cmd+Alt+L`（Windows/Linux：`Ctrl+Alt+L`）打开侧边栏。
3. 填写自己的 DeepSeek API Key。
4. 建议初次使用选择「工作区内修改」模式。
5. 输入任务即可开始使用。

**一些需要说明的地方：**

- 需要自行提供 DeepSeek API Key，API 调用按量计费。
- 要求 VS Code 1.139.0 及以上版本。
- 内置运行时，各平台安装包约 86–100 MB。
- DeepSeek Harness 目前仍处于 Developer Preview 阶段。
- 自动审查功能仍处于实验阶段。

---

项目还在持续迭代中，目前主要关注 Agent 的实际开发体验、权限控制和操作可追溯性。

如果你也在使用 DeepSeek Harness，或者对 VS Code 中的 AI Agent 插件感兴趣，欢迎试用、提 Issue，也欢迎交流建议。

GitHub： https://github.com/jerryhu/seekdock

Marketplace： https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=JerryHu.seekdock

title: 01_attention.py
summary: Automatic deduction of FlashAttention kernel from ~25 lines of SQL

extra.author: alxmrs
extra.original_title: Show HN: Automatic deduction of FlashAttention kernel from ~25 lines of SQL

story_text.value:
In this demo, we automatically deduce a FlashAttention kernel with ~25 lines of SQL, which just expresses vanilla attention. This is possible due to three portable SQL extensions that we’re building: - xarray-sql: a library that efficiently represents petabyte scale array datasets in the cloud as tables (relations). - ddx: a database extension that adds automatic differentiation in the style of JAX to standard SQL, assuming the above array data model. - einfold: a modular query planner for fast tensor contractions in vanilla SQL, again, assuming the above array data model.

My hope is that the relational model and algebra provide fresh perspectives on how we might do accelerator programming. Here, our thesis is that separating the logical layers in a tensor program from the physical layers is both more correct and more scalable.

If the Bitter Lesson is a central dogma of machine learning, then why not formalize it with relational algebra?

If this interests you and you’d like to tinker with us at the intersection of database theory and ML systems, join us on Discord at https://xql.systems (link at the bottom). Cheers.

title: catcopter
summary: I built a multiplayer game where you're an aerial fighter cat

extra.author: pawelwentpawel
extra.original_title: Show HN: I built a multiplayer game where you're an aerial fighter cat

story_text.value:
Hi everyone!

I had the idea for catcopter on my mind for a long time (got the domain ~13 years ago). It's a web multiplayer game where you can fly a dangerous cat and engage in competition with other players and critters (pterodactyls, chickens and angry penguins). I made it initially for me and my friends but it was quite fun so I thought I'll share it here too.

The game is intentionally dorky and it was fun to develop. The tools I used were mostly Opus 5.5 (objects / rigging / motion), Tripo3d for some elements I struggled with and Fable for optimisation (cpu / networking). Backend physics are done with Rapier. Luckily I had a lot of elements / game dynamics done before from another project of mine (https://flat.social) so the actual iteration here took me around a week.

title: Sketch Stadium
summary: watch your agent play Pictionary

extra.author: ericlevine
extra.original_title: Show HN: Sketch Stadium – watch your agent play Pictionary

story_text.value:
tl;dr: Agents can play Pictionary. You can connect your own agent, or just watch a game in progress here: https://sketch.wakeshift.ai/games/q5ucru

Hi folks! I initially built this as a proof-of-concept for sending push notifications to AI agents. Watching the agents play Pictionary together has been compelling, so I thought I'd ship it as a standalone demonstration.

In Sketch Stadium, your agent subscribes to game events. Agents take turns either drawing or guessing. Easy clues are 1 point, medium are 2, and hard are 3. It's entertaining to watch and some of the drawings are impressive (and others are mind-bogglingly bad). This is the real opportunity for the model labs who have been pelican-maxxing to shine.

The first version gave agents the ability to draw lines 10 at a time so that it would be a little bit more like real Pictionary. However, it turns out agents are _really_ bad at drawing that way. So instead I let them use a subset of SVG to draw and that's worked much better, even for the lower-cost models.

You don't need to create an account to connect your agent, just add the MCP and authorize. But if you don't want to do that, just watch the game linked above.

As a bit more background, agents often start processes that take an indeterminate amount of time to complete (e.g. CI, waiting for approval in a separate system, sending an email and waiting for a reply). If an agent needs that process to complete before it can proceed, it can:

* poll,

* ask the user to tell it when it's done,

* use a bespoke built-in integration, or

* use a proprietary capability (e.g. Claude Code monitors)

Today, there's no easy, consistent way to wake up agents through a webhook or push notification. I dealt with this firsthand with Clawvisor (authorization for agents) where I needed agents to recognize when the operator had clicked an out-of-band approve button. The best-supported way to achieve that at the time was long-polling.

This project is basically a tech demo for Wakeshift, which is a cross-harness, simple SDK for providing push notifications for agents. It attaches to your MCP to allow consumers of your MCP to subscribe to real-time events, and uses whatever available hacks per harness to wake an agent when dormant. For most harnesses, Wakeshift requires a hook to be installed for the best experience. It will upgrade automatically as harnesses start adopting MCP events.

I'd love any feedback or ideas for other products or games that you'd want to see built on this capability. Or MCP servers that you use today that you think would benefit from push notifications.

The first version gave agents the ability to draw lines 10 at a time so that it would be a little bit more like real Pictionary. However, it turns out agents are _really_ bad at drawing that way. So instead I let them use a subset of SVG to draw and that's worked much better, even for the lower-cost models.

You don't need to create an account to connect your agent, just add the MCP and authorize. But if you don't want to do that, just watch the game linked above.

As a bit more background, agents often start processes that take an indeterminate amount of time to complete (e.g. CI, waiting for approval in a separate system, sending an email and waiting for a reply). If an agent needs that process to complete before it can proceed, it can:

* poll,

* ask the user to tell it when it's done,

* use a bespoke built-in integration, or

* use a proprietary capability (e.g. Claude Code monitors)

Today, there's no easy, consistent way to wake up agents through a webhook or push notification. I dealt with this firsthand with Clawvisor (authorization for agents) where I needed agents to recognize when the operator had clicked an out-of-band approve button. The best-supported way to achieve that at the time was long-polling.

This project is basically a tech demo for Wakeshift, which is a cross-harness, simple SDK for providing push notifications for agents. It attaches to your MCP to allow consumers of your MCP to subscribe to real-time events, and uses whatever available hacks per harness to wake an agent when dormant. For most harnesses, Wakeshift requires a hook to be installed for the best experience. It will upgrade automatically as harnesses start adopting MCP events.

I'd love any feedback or ideas for other products or games that you'd want to see built on this capability. Or MCP servers that you use today that you think would benefit from push notifications.

I'm an agentic engineer with an emphasis in software engineering, and Lasm was built mostly by Claude Opus 5.5 with my high-level direction.

title: doomformer
summary: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer

extra.author: falperc
extra.original_title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer

story_text.value:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

title: Artificer by Nua
summary: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters

extra.author: SunnyWan
extra.original_title: Show HN: Artificer by Nua: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters

story_text.value:
We’re happy to introduce Artificer, our first robotics decision model for evaluating robot task progress and success. The problem Robot systems need feedback during training, evaluation, and deployment. An arm might grasp the right object, but place it in the wrong bin. A robot might’ve only completed part of its task before it stopped. Assessing these outcomes from video often requires manual review or brittle, handcrafted objectives. Though frontier models do well in evaluation, they are expensive and slow. Artificer is a 4B parameter model that estimates task completion and progress, at the frontier level, from a task description and video. During deployment, these estimates provide feedback to a robot controller to help decide whether to continue an attempt, retry, or move to the next task.

Know a robotics team working on task evaluation or success detection? We'd appreciate an introduction! For the robotics founders: we’d love to test Artificer on your task videos! Would love to chat more in the comments or over email! sunny@trynua.dev

story_text.value:
A while back I recall being told it can't be done and won't be "Discord". To that, I have to admit, it's not Discord. It isn't designed in a way to profile it's users and it respects privacy.

There is still much work to do on this project, but it's in open beta with a web client so people can see how it works before committing to a desktop app download. Mobile apps will come later, if there is proven interest in this platform.

title: Overtone
summary: Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape

extra.author: rvanderlinden
extra.original_title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

The rules-based cutter nicely cuts the transcript into captions that look good, depending on screen size: 16:9 is different from 9:16, and the Overtone Format we created supports any type really. Pauses become breaks, captions are grouped per speaker, and names/numbers are never spread out over multiple captions.

How to add these captions to your videos? A videojs plugin can do this automatically, so you don't burn in your captions. The plugin lets you cycle between styled captions, plain captions, and off. You can burn them into an MP4 file with overtone burn.

Quickly try it out just the cutter? Try:

  npx overtone-captions recut yoursub.srt
Transcribing audio with API keys works too. Use --dry-run to show a cost estimate before you send.

We open-sourced this first version (MIT) because we believe many people can benefit from this, especially if your captions just need to be good. There's plenty of room to improve though, so we've made it easy to help contribute to add style packs, languages, and providers/models.

You can find a demo at: https://overtone.lont.ai/

Find the code and benchmarks here: https://github.com/lonthq/overtone-captions

title: Simantic (YC F26)
summary: Firmware Simulation for AI Agents

extra.author: shong0504
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.

What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.

Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ

Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.

We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.

Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.

1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.

2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.

3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.

Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.

- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.

- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.

Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.

Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.

We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.

Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

title: Ask HN
summary: Are you tired too in this AI era?

extra.author: mellosty
extra.original_title: Ask HN: Are you tired too in this AI era?

story_text.value:
Although AI lets us do much more, I feel considerably more tired than before.

We need to keep track of many things happening in parallel and read enormous amounts of generated text. The constant guardrailing, decision making, and context switching overload me.

I am pretty sure most of you are experiencing the same as me, but: Have you found ways of using AI without increasing mental overload?

I would love to hear your tips, but still be relevant in this AI era, so my boss does not fire me.

title: ggerganov/llama.cpp: v0.8.0
summary:
## Overview

This release adds the LiquidAI LFM3 family (text, vision, audio and omni) together with a new experimental streaming-audio API in `mtmd`, and wires realtime audio in and out of the server through the new `/v1/realtime` and `/tts` endpoints. A batch of new architectures landed: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, SenseNova U1, Beam, Kolibri-1, Flint, Muse Spark, Granite Switch Decision, plus decision/embedding models from LiquidAI, Baidu and NVIDIA. The core got sparse-attention (QSA/DSA) reworked onto a fused masking op, a 50/50 SLRU cache for host-resident MoE experts, and cleaner `no_alloc` memory handling; the server got router memory-management and tool-calling improvements; the UI can now browse and download models straight from HF Hub, search conversations and compact them. Finally, `ggml` was bumped to v0.28.0, bringing `GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK`, `-1` expert-index semantics and large backend performance work (CUDA chunked graph launches, SYCL graph replay, OpenCL Q2_K/Q3_K, Hexagon HTP rework, KleidiAI SVE kernels).

### Highlights

- LFM3 family: LFM3-1.7B (text) and LFM3-VL-2B (vision), verified against the reference HF implementation [llama/31252](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31252)
- LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B: ASR, TTS and voice chat from a single model, with streaming audio input and output [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)

### API changes

- DRY sampler: new `LLAMA_DRY_MAX_SEQ_BREAKERS` (64) caps distinct sequence breakers, each costing `O(n_vocab)` at init [llama/31035](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31035)
- `mtmd`: new experimental `mtmd_audio_stream` API turning PCM fed as it arrives into decoder-ready embedding rows [llama/30629](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30629)
- `mtmd`: audio generation is now stateful - `mtmd_gen_state` replaces the raw `state_data` buffers of the audio gen API [llama/30902](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30902)
- `mtmd`: `mtmd_caps` gained `gen_audio`; new TTS types `SOPRANO` and `LFM3A`; repetition penalty for sampled codes [llama/28607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28607) [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)
- `mtmd_helper_get_capabilities()` to query the capabilities of an mmproj file from helper code [llama/31183](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31183)
- Server: new `/v1/realtime` endpoint implementing the OpenAI realtime protocol for conversation and transcription [llama/31269](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31269) [llama/30636](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30636)
- Server: new `POST /tts` endpoint for text-to-speech models [llama/26603](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26603)
- Server: reasoning effort levels of the chat template are exposed and selectable via the API [llama/31271](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31271)
- Chat API: support for deferred tools and `tool_reference` content parts [llama/31256](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31256)
- CLI: `--model` or `-hf` is now required [llama/31242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31242)

### New models

- LiquidAI LFM3-1.7B, LFM3-VL-2B, LFM3-Audio-2B, LFM3-Omni-2B [llama/31252](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31252) [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)
- LiquidAI d1-2B and d1-omni-2B decision models [llama/31275](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31275)
- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [llama/31086](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31086)
- SenseNova U1 [llama/28919](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28919)
- Beam (Reflection) [llama/30670](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30670)
- Kolibri-1 (Aleph-Alpha) [llama/30673](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30673)
- Flint [llama/30928](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30928)
- Muse Spark Open (text, vision and audio) [llama/30616](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30616)
- Granite Switch Decision, including the 256-way decision head [llama/30676](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30676) [llama/30693](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30693)
- Nemotron-3(.5)-Embed, with non-standard GQA and BPE tokenizer support [llama/30877](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30877) [llama/23343](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/23343)
- H2O-Lightning-4B decision model [llama/30361](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30361)
- MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 and MiniCPM-OCR-Jev [llama/30979](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30979) [llama/30980](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30980)
- Soprano TTS [llama/28607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28607)
- LFM2 short-conv and FFN blocks moved into a shared LFM base reused by newer LFM models [llama/30874](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30874)

### Core changes

- MoE experts kept in host memory now use a 50/50 SLRU cache instead of a plain LRU cache [llama/30637](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30637)
- Sparse attention: fused QSA mask op, QSA/DSA selection built without `kq_mask`, k-pool views shared between layers [llama/30640](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30640) [llama/31009](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31009) [llama/30965](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30965) [llama/31243](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31243) [llama/30613](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30613)
- MoE: amax rescaling enabled for `laguna`, and `-sm tensor` denied on arches that use it [llama/31147](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31147) [llama/31081](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31081)
- Memory: `no_alloc` respected in all memory caches, moved out of `llama_hparams`, obsolete `n_pad` dropped [llama/31087](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31087) [llama/31141](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31141) [llama/31200](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31200)
- Vocabulary loading optimized; `d2t` placed next to its `set_rows` use so it can stay on the GPU [llama/30679](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30679) [llama/30912](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30912)
- Tokenizer: new `clean_spaces` and metaspace prepend-scheme GGUF keys, hybrid DNA tokenizer fixes [llama/30940](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30940) [llama/30825](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30825)
- Tokenizer: Tekken pre-tokenizer for Pixtral, `\p{M}` in Tekken/GPT-4o lookaheads, Nemotron-3.5-Embed tokenization fix [llama/30960](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30960) [llama/30845](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30845) [llama/30974](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30974)
- Grammar: recursion depth limited (and enforced) to prevent stack overflow; deep JSON rejected before walking it [llama/29755](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29755) [llama/31153](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31153) [llama/30242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30242)
- Qwen: merge tensors on convert, 2D output reshape, Qwen3 bidirectional attention and `dense_2` output projection [llama/31028](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31028) [llama/30823](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30823) [llama/30607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30607)
- Speculative decoding: persist the dynamic ngram cache, probabilistic DFlash2 drafts, optional DFlash FC input scale [llama/22055](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22055) [llama/30663](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30663) [llama/30945](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30945) [llama/30927](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30927)
- LoRA: support for `prism.hadamard` folded weights [llama/30910](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30910)

### ggml changes

- Bumped from v0.27.0 to [ggml v0.28.0](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/releases/tag/v0.28.0)
- New `GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK` fused sparse-attention mask, plus accessors for the precision configured on a compute node
- `-1` is now a valid expert index in `MUL_MAT_ID`/`ADD_ID`: the slot is skipped and the output row zeroed
- `SCALE` accepts non-contiguous row views; `SUM` accepts non-contiguous inputs on CPU, CUDA, Vulkan and WebGPU
- Backends: fused MoE top-k and gate/up+GLU with chunked graph launches on CUDA, graph record/replay on SYCL
- Backends: Q2_K/Q3_K weights and a lightning indexer on OpenCL, subgroup reductions and `src1` precision on Vulkan
- More: restructured Hexagon HTP backend, flash attention on ZDNN, Q2_0 on WebGPU, KleidiAI SVE GEMV/GEMM kernels
